name: Hilarion of Gaza
knownFor: Antony's disciple, remembered as the first monk of Palestine, who brought the Egyptian desert life to the coast near Gaza.
place: Thabatha, near Gaza, and later Cyprus
role: Hermit and founder of Palestinian monasticism

traces: Monastic life on the Palestinian coast, which Jerome credits him with originating: "It was he who originated this mode of life and devotion."
The conversion of families near Gaza, among them that of Sozomen's own grandfather, which Sozomen traces to Hilarion's cure of Alaphion.
remembered: Jerome of Strido wrote his Life about 390 and set him beside Antony: "The Lord Jesus had in Egypt the aged Antony: in Palestine He had the youthful Hilarion."
Epiphanius of Salamis, who knew him, had already "set forth his praises in a short but widely circulated letter," by Jerome's account.

uncertain: Hilarion left no writing that is held here. His life is known chiefly from Jerome's Life, a work of praise. The editor of Jerome's works warns that it "contains, amidst much that is legendary, some statements which attach it to genuine history."
Sozomen, whose own family came from the region, gives an independent notice of Hilarion and of the cure of Alaphion. He drew in part on Jerome's Life and diverges from it on some points.
His dates rest on the Life and on Sozomen. Jerome says he died in his eightieth year, having served Christ "nearly seventy years."
